title: The Curse Psalms
lead: Some psalms ask God to punish, shame or destroy the speaker's enemies (for example Psalms 35, 69, 109 and 137, with shorter curses in many others). Jews and Christians have prayed them, softened them, read them as prayers against evil itself, or left them out of worship.

sections.h: What the curse psalms ask for
sections.b: A curse psalm is usually a lament. The speaker is attacked, accused or betrayed, and asks God to act as judge: to shame the attackers, turn their traps back on them, or wipe them out. The speaker almost never takes revenge in person. The prayer hands vengeance to God, as the law of Moses does (Deuteronomy 32:35). Longer examples are Psalms 35, 69, 109 and 137; shorter curses come in Psalms 5, 10, 28, 58, 59, 83, 139 and 140.
